Initially, the wheel will slip and spin. When the slipping stops, the friction force directed along the wheel plane disappears, but a certain force remains acting perpendicular to it, tending to steer the wheel sideways. This force is essentially static friction. Its origin is the deformation of the tire near the contact patch. The presence of this force causes the car to turn, i.e., the sum of slip forces acting on each wheel of the car is the centripetal force. Thus, when turning, the wheel plane is always slightly turned relative to the velocity vector of the wheel center (the wheels do not go where they "look").
